You speak of neighbours, spirit, but my scouts have walked the woods and the shores and seen no village called Wewush. Our granary is full of golden wheat, yes, and Gujia does not grudge food to empty bellies if the hand that takes it is peaceful. But tell me—where do these people make their fire, how many days' march are they from our waters, and why have our own eyes never met theirs upon the trail? Show me the path to their hearths, or I must believe your words are only smoke drifting in the night.

You speak of Wewush, spirit, but my scouts have walked many days through forest and shore, and no living man of Ilkei has ever seen this place or sat by their fires. We have plenty of grain in our granary, and we do not turn a hungry stranger from our hearth, but I cannot send our people hauling heavy carts into the mist for a folk known only in a dream. 

Tell me, then: where do these neighbours lie? How many suns must a man walk, and in which direction, before he smells the smoke of Wewush? Bring me a true path to walk, and we shall see if their bellies need filling. Until then, my grain stays dry under our roof.

You speak of people we have never seen. Our scouts have walked many days into the marsh, along the shores, and under the trees, and have found no village called Joawethom. 

Our granary is full because our hands worked the dirt and hauled the nets, not because grain falls like rain. I will not send good wheat into the mist after names from a dream. 

Tell me, shadow—where do these people light their fires, and what path leads to their door? If they are flesh and bone, let them send walkers of their own to our huts, and we will talk as men talk. Until then, my people keep what they have reaped.
